claims.text: A closed-loop framework for LLM coding agents codifies every accepted human review comment as a persistent behavioral rule in a version-controlled instruction file, so the agent progressively self-detects more error classes.

The closed-loop coding-agent framework combines an accumulating rule set in a version-controlled instruction file, a self-review checklist executed before code submission, and automated validation of rule-set integrity as it grows.

In deployment across a 35+ service microservices platform, the rule set grew from 5 to 18 behavioral rules, 15+ language-specific standards, and a 15-item self-review checklist, all derived from real review feedback.
The framework's memory content is derived exclusively from accepted review outcomes, and each new rule is traceable to a specific accepted comment.
The framework converts point corrections into class-level constraints, but it prevents only known failure modes, not all possible failures, and does not prove semantic correctness.
In one 16-agent reference system, tokens per query grew from 4K to 12K in three weeks from accumulated context (prompt bloat), tripling latency and cost.
In the same reference system, a context optimizer (dedupe, semantic chunking, relevance scoring, query-type assembly, priority loading) yielded 50-60% fewer tokens in the author's own testing.
Reflective memory in the reference system triggers a reflection when the same error occurs 3 or more times, stores an insight, and later records an effectiveness score for the fix.
The reflection agent in the reference system iterates up to 3 times, stopping early if quality reaches 0.9; the author reports diminishing returns beyond 3 iterations.

In the reference system, a meta-prompt agent combines reflective-memory error signals with procedural-memory workflow gaps to rewrite a specialist agent's prompt without human intervention, and tracks which prompt versions perform best.

The author of the reference system reports that the same misclassification recurred across three weeks, with each failure looking isolated, because no structured memory existed to reveal the pattern; these results are self-reported from the author's own testing, not independent evaluation.

Procedural memory in the reference system records tool sequences, success/failure and response time in PostgreSQL, and recommends workflows ranked by historical success rate; the author reports it found the best tool sequence per query type after 200 test cases.
Explicit procedural memory (system prompt rules, playbooks, skills, validated runbooks) should be written through a deliberate promotion step with validation rather than a fully automatic write path.

A suggested two-tier design keeps agent-written candidate procedures in a `candidates/` area and promotes them to a live `playbooks/` area only through a validation gate, preventing silent self-modification of the agent's operating rules.
Procedural memory should be loaded just-in-time rather than by stuffing every rule into every prompt, and it needs versioning and deprecation rather than deletion.
LangChain's LangMem treats procedural memory as prompt rules that are updated over time based on feedback.
Episodic memory should expire on a TTL and semantic memory needs staleness checks because facts change; stale tool outputs in long contexts can actively mislead an agent.
Arize's guide says a memory system that never forgets compounds old mistakes more often than useful knowledge, so memory records need versioning, freshness rules and deletion rules.
Arize lists the main regression risks of prompt changes as instruction conflicts and prompt bloat, and of memory changes as wrong or outdated context becoming persistent.

Arize recommends validating a candidate change against the same dataset and evaluator versions as the baseline, including unrelated canary cases so a targeted fix cannot hide a broader regression, and keeping a rollback artifact.
Arize advises automating narrow, clearly measured changes more aggressively than permissions, safety policy, spend controls or model weights.
Reflection becomes a validated improvement only after an independent comparison shows the saved lesson helps; automatic proposal and automatic promotion are different autonomy levels.

The Fragility study re-evaluated memory-based self-improvement methods Agent Workflow Memory and ReasoningBank using repeated runs across WebArena (812 tasks), VisualWebArena (910 tasks) and SCUBA (267 tasks) to separate signal from noise.
The ACE paper (Zhang et al., 2025) treats context as a playbook grown through small incremental edits and names 'context collapse', where repeated rewriting erodes detail.
Persistent notes such as AGENTS.md only help if they are actually injected into future prompts; some tools do not auto-load files like progress.txt, so teams should verify the notes are included.
